practices.body: Before one specific act of obedience this week, say what is powering it. If the honest answer is fear of losing standing, do it anyway — and then preach the verdict to yourself until the fuel changes.

practices.title: FIND WHAT CUT IN
practices.body: You were running well at some point. Trace back to when it changed and name the thing that broke up the road — a teaching, a friendship, a season of failure. Say it to one person who can help you get back on the track.

practices.title: KEEP THE OFFENSE
practices.body: Identify the clause of the gospel you file down most often to make conversation easier. Say it unsoftened once this week. The stumbling block is not a flaw in the message; it is the message.

title: Stand Firm in Freedom
subtitle: from dust to faith working through love
keyVerse: Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.

passage.text: Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.
Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you receive circumcision, Christ will profit you nothing.
Yes, I testify again to every man who receives circumcision that he is a debtor to do the whole law.
You are alienated from Christ, you who desire to be justified by the law. You have fallen away from grace.
For we, through the Spirit, by faith wait for the hope of righteousness.
For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision amounts to anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.
You were running well! Who interfered with you that you should not obey the truth?
This persuasion is not from him who calls you.
A little yeast grows through the whole lump.
I have confidence toward you in the Lord that you will think no other way. But he who troubles you will bear his judgment, whoever he is.
But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? Then the stumbling block of the cross has been removed.
I wish that those who disturb you would cut themselves off.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about learning to tell two voices apart, and about refusing a yoke that was taken off your neck at Calvary and has no business being put back on.
lifePulls: The cross is hated not because it is obscure but because it is insulting — it tells the accomplished man and the ruined man that they arrive on identical terms.
prayer: Lord Jesus, You have made me free, and You took the yoke off my neck at Calvary. I will not put it back on today. Teach me to tell Your voice from the accuser’s: Yours names my sin and sends me to You; his leaves me hiding. Let my obedience today run on love, not fear, and let my faith do its work through love. Amen.
prayerLines: Lord Jesus, You have made me free,
and You took the yoke off my neck at Calvary.
I will not put it back on today.
Teach me to tell Your voice from the accuser’s:
Yours names my sin and sends me to You;
his leaves me hiding.
Let my obedience today run on love, not fear,
and let my faith do its work through love. Amen.
bottomLine: Everything in the letter comes to rest on one command, and the command stands on a finished work: Christ has made you free, so stand firm. Take up the law as your acceptance and you are a debtor to the whole of it, cut off from the only power that was working in you. What counts in Christ is “faith working through love,” and the offense of the cross stays, because every man comes to God with empty hands.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the yoke someone has been sliding back onto your neck and onto the One who took it off. You have been listening to a voice that sounds like conscience and is not. It never names a specific sin. It never points to a remedy. It never once leaves you running toward God. Learn its accent. It has been wearing you down for years.

And hear the order of Paul’s command, because it is the order of everything. Christ has made us free — that first, finished, accomplished without your assistance. Therefore stand firm. He does not tell you to fight your way toward liberty. He tells a freed man to stop accepting chains from people who have no right to offer them.

So stop trying to keep one foot in each economy. You cannot draw on both accounts, and the attempt is precisely what has left you exhausted — disconnected from the only current that was ever working, while insisting you were being responsible. Grace is not fragile. But it does not run on a circuit you are trying to power yourself.

Then go and work — not to buy anything, but because faith cannot sit still and love is what it discharges through. That is the whole Christian ethic in four words, and it is the reason grace has never produced a lazy man it truly reached. Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to, and stand where Christ has already put you.
closingVerse: Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.
carry: Whose voice have you been obeying that names no sin, offers no remedy, and leaves you hiding?

paras: Every man who has taken grace seriously has eventually met the accusation: if God accepts you apart from your performance, what is to stop you doing as you please? It is the oldest charge against the gospel, and the fact that it gets raised is usually a sign the gospel has been preached accurately.

But the more dangerous version of the question is not the one asked by critics. It is the one a man asks himself at the end of a bad month, when the same sin has come back for the fifth time and he cannot tell whether he is a believer with a struggle or a fraud with a vocabulary.

Here is where the dust lies to you. It reads the struggle inside you as evidence of your condition — as though the presence of conflict meant the absence of the Spirit. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has been losing that argument: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV).
And the reviving word of Galatians 5 is that before conversion there was no struggle, because the flesh had the field to itself.

sections.heading: Freedom With a Direction
pulls: Before conversion the flesh had the field to itself. The struggle you feel is proof that a second life has been planted.
paras: For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.

Paul does not retreat an inch on the freedom. He restates it in the same breath that he guards it. And the word he uses for the danger is aphormē — a starting point, an opening. The flesh will happily use your liberty as a place to start from if you let it.

Then comes the alternative nobody expects: through love be servants to one another. The verb is douleuō — be slaves. Paul has spent five chapters getting these men out of slavery and now hands them a yoke.

But it is a different yoke entirely. You were freed from bondage to sin and law so that you could become, voluntarily and gladly, a servant of your brother. Freedom in the Bible is never freedom from all obligation. It is freedom from the wrong master so that you can serve the right one.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE LAW FULFILLED IN ONE WORD
paras: For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
This should stop a legalist in his tracks. Paul, who has spent four chapters removing the law as a means of acceptance, now says the whole of it is fulfilled — and the fulfillment is love.

The men demanding law-keeping were, in fact, failing at the law. Paul says so bluntly in the next verse: but if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another. The language is of wild animals tearing at each other.

That is what legalism does to a congregation, and it is not accidental. When acceptance is earned, other men stop being family and become competition. Your brother’s failure improves your standing. Grace is the only soil in which a church can stop eating itself.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE STRUGGLE THAT PROVES YOU ARE ALIVE
paras: For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.
Every honest Christian recognizes that sentence, and it is important to understand what it signifies. The conflict is not evidence that something has gone wrong with you.

Before conversion there was no contest. There was appetite and there was consequence, but nothing else was growing in that field — nothing inside a man that genuinely grieved over his sin as sin rather than over its cost. The struggle you feel is proof that a second life has been planted.

So do not read your struggle as disqualification. Read it as new growth. The very fact that the gap between what you are and what you want to be causes you pain is the Spirit at work, because the flesh has never once been troubled by that gap.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: WORKS PLURAL, FRUIT SINGULAR
paras: Now Paul sets two lists side by side, and the grammar is doing theological work.

The deeds of the flesh are plural — a scattered catalog of appetites pulling a man in different directions at once. Adultery, idolatry, hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions, envy, drunkenness. There is no unity to it. It is a man coming apart.

The fruit of the Spirit is singular. Not fruits. One organic thing, grown rather than manufactured, arriving as a unit. You cannot select patience and decline self-control the way you would order from a menu.

And bottom line, the fruit of the Spirit is love — joy and peace and patience and kindness and goodness and faith and gentleness and self-control are the qualities of that love. Read 1 Corinthians 13 beside this list and you will see the same portrait. And it is finally a portrait of Christ. The Spirit is not producing generic virtue in you. He is forming the character of the Son.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: CRUCIFIED, AND KEEPING IN STEP
paras: Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.

Note how the flesh is dealt with. Not managed, not negotiated with, not put on a schedule. Crucified. It is a slow, deliberate, and utterly fatal business, and it is spoken of as something already done to those who belong to Christ.

Which is why verse twenty-five gives the command it does: If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit. The verb pictures rows in a field, or men walking in line — keeping in line, in step, neither straining ahead nor lagging behind.

Two verbs sit side by side here and they must be held together. In verse twenty-four something was accomplished when you were joined to Christ. In verse twenty-five something is commanded of you every day, deliberately, one decision at a time. God works in you — therefore work out what He is working in. His sovereignty is the reason for your effort, never the substitute for it.

stations.verse: For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.
stations.question: Where have I let my liberty become an opening for the very thing Christ freed me from?
stations.gloss: a starting point; an occasion or opening
body: Aphormē is a starting point — the place something sets out from. In war it named a base of operations; in the New Testament it means an occasion, an opening, the ground a thing works from.

Paul uses it in Romans of sin seizing an opportunity through the commandment. Here the opportunity is your freedom itself. The flesh cannot attack from nothing; it needs ground to work from, and grace misused makes excellent terrain.
Which is why Paul guards liberty rather than withdrawing it. He does not say be less free. He says do not hand the flesh a foothold on ground Christ purchased for you.
stations.live: Name the freedom you have been using as cover for something. Do not surrender the freedom — evict the tenant.

stations.verse: But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another.
stations.question: Whose failure have I quietly enjoyed because it made me look better by comparison?
stations.gloss: to bite; to wound as an animal tearing at flesh
stations.xref: GALATIANS 5:15 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT
body: Daknō is the literal word for an animal’s bite, and Paul pairs it with two more from the same field: devour, which is used of wild beasts swallowing prey, and consume, which means to finish off entirely. The whole sentence is a picture of a pack turning on itself.
He is describing a church. Not a mob, not the world outside — a congregation of men who had been arguing about circumcision and had begun tearing at each other over it.

And the logic is exact. Where acceptance is earned, your brother’s standing threatens your own, and his failure quietly improves your position. Legalism does not merely produce anxious men. It produces hungry ones.
stations.live: Find the man whose stumble you were secretly glad to hear about. Confess it to God by name, and then do something for him this week.

stations.verse: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
stations.question: Am I trying to manufacture virtues — or staying attached to the source that grows them?
stations.gloss: fruit; what a living thing produces naturally out of its own nature
body: Karpos is the ordinary word for produce — what grows on a tree. And Paul’s choice is deliberate, because he has just called the opposite list works. Works are manufactured. Fruit is grown.

Note the number. Works of the flesh, plural; fruit of the Spirit, singular. Nine qualities named, one fruit. It arrives as a unit, the way an apple does not offer you its sweetness while withholding its color.

And fruit is never produced by the branch straining. Jesus said it plainly: abide in me — he who remains in me bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. Your job is not to generate patience out of nothing. It is to stay attached.
stations.live: Stop working on one virtue this week by willpower. Instead give that time to abiding — word, prayer, the Lord’s table — and let the branch do what branches do.

stations.verse: gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
stations.question: Do I have any inner mastery that is not simply fear of consequences?
stations.gloss: self-control; mastery exercised from within, holding oneself in hand
body: Enkrateia joins en, in, to kratos, strength or dominion. It means holding power over oneself — the same root behind words for ruling and gripping. It was a prized virtue in Greek moral philosophy, achieved by discipline.

Paul puts it last on a list of things the Spirit grows. That placement is the whole point. The pagan moralist made self-control the foundation of the virtuous life, produced by effort. Paul makes it fruit — the ninth quality of a single love, grown rather than achieved.

Which does not mean a Christian exerts no effort. It means his self-mastery has a different root system. Restraint driven by fear of consequences collapses the moment the consequences are removed. Restraint grown by the Spirit holds in the dark.
stations.live: Identify one restraint in your life that would collapse if no one were watching. Bring it to God this week as something to be grown, not merely enforced.

stations.verse: If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
stations.question: Where am I straining ahead of God, or lagging behind Him, instead of keeping step?
stations.gloss: to be in a row; to walk in line; to keep in step
body: Stoicheō comes from stoichos, a row or rank — the same root as the stoicheia of chapter four. But where those were the elementary rudiments men were held under, this is the verb for walking in an ordered line.
It is not the general word for walking; Paul used that one in verse sixteen. This is specific: to keep in line, in step with those beside you, neither pushing ahead nor falling behind.

And that is a striking picture of sanctification. Not sprinting, not being carried, but matching pace with Someone. The Spirit sets the rhythm. Your part is to keep it — which requires attention every day and heroics on almost none of them.
stations.live: Ask honestly whether you are straining ahead of God or dragging behind Him this season. Then take one step at His pace today instead of yours.

practices.title: READ THE STRUGGLE RIGHTLY
practices.body: Write down the struggle that most makes you doubt yourself. Then write beside it what Paul says it means: a second life has been planted in the field. The flesh has never once grieved over sin as sin. Your grief is evidence, not disqualification.

practices.title: EVICT THE TENANT
practices.body: Name the freedom you have been using as cover for something the flesh wanted. Do not surrender the liberty — Paul does not — but take back the ground you have let it use.

practices.title: STOP MANUFACTURING ONE VIRTUE
practices.body: Pick the quality you have been trying hardest to produce by willpower. Give that effort to abiding instead this week — word, prayer, the table, the fellowship of God’s people — and let the branch do what branches do.

practices.title: CONFESS THE COMPARISON
practices.body: Find the brother whose stumble you were quietly glad to hear about. That instinct is what Paul calls biting. Confess it by name to God, and then do something concrete for the man this week.

practices.title: MATCH THE PACE
practices.body: Ask whether you are straining ahead of God or lagging behind Him this season. Both break step. Take one step today at His pace — no heroics, no stalling — and do the same tomorrow.

title: Walk by the Spirit
subtitle: from dust to the fruit of the Spirit
keyVerse: If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.

passage.text: For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.
For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another.
But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.
For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.
But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
Now the deeds of the flesh are obvious, which are: adultery, sexual immorality, uncleanness, lustfulness,
idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions, heresies,
envy, murders, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these; of which I forewarn you, even as I also forewarned you, that those who practice such things will not inherit God’s Kingdom.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about reading your inner conflict correctly, and about trading manufacture for cultivation — because works are made and fruit is grown.
lifePulls: Fruit is never produced by the branch straining. Your job is not to generate patience out of nothing. It is to stay attached.
prayer: Holy Spirit, You have taken up ground the flesh used to hold alone. When the struggle comes back, let me read it rightly: not as proof that You have left, but as proof that You are here. I will not manufacture what only You can grow. Keep me attached to Christ, and keep me in step with You today — not ahead, not behind. Amen.
prayerLines: Holy Spirit, You have taken up ground
the flesh used to hold alone.
When the struggle comes back, let me read it rightly:
not as proof that You have left,
but as proof that You are here.
I will not manufacture what only You can grow.
Keep me attached to Christ,
and keep me in step with You today —
not ahead, not behind. Amen.
bottomLine: You were called for freedom, but the flesh will use that freedom as an opening if you let it; so through love, serve one another. The struggle you feel is not proof that you are a fraud — it is proof that the Spirit has moved in. Works of the flesh are many and manufactured; the fruit of the Spirit is one, and it is grown.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the struggle you have been reading as a verdict and onto the One whose presence explains it. You have been counting the same failure a fifth time and concluding that a real Christian would not still be here. But look at what the struggle actually proves. Before Christ, the flesh had your field to itself. Before Christ, nothing in you grieved over sin as sin. Before Christ, there was one crop and no contest. The grief you feel is new life pushing up through ground the flesh used to own.

So stop demanding of yourself a fruit you were never asked to manufacture. Works are made; fruit is grown. Nobody has ever produced patience by clenching, and the branch that strains hardest is not the one that bears. Your calling is quieter and harder than effort: stay attached. Abide. The life runs from the vine to the branch and the fruit comes because it must.

And notice what the Spirit is actually growing. Not generic decency. Love — and joy and peace and patience and kindness and goodness and faith and gentleness and self-control are that love wearing nine faces. Set the list beside the Gospels and you will see whose portrait it is. He is forming the character of the Son in a man made of dust.

So keep in step today. Not sprinting ahead of God to prove something, not lagging behind Him out of discouragement, but matching His pace one ordinary step at a time. The flesh was crucified when you were joined to Christ; you are not negotiating with a living thing. Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to, and walk in step with the Spirit who moved in.
closingVerse: If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
carry: What have you been reading as evidence against yourself that Paul would have you read as proof the Spirit has taken up residence?

paras: There is a particular loneliness that belongs to men who believe the right things. He has the doctrine. He can explain justification. And he is carrying something he has never told anyone, because the group he belongs to has made it clear — without ever saying so — that men like them do not have problems like his.

So he manages it alone. He prays about it alone. And every week he sits in a room full of people who would help him if they knew, and does not tell them, because he has calculated the cost of being known and decided he cannot afford it.

Here is where the dust lies to you. It tells you that carrying it alone is strength, and that the weight you cannot put down is proof you do not belong. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul under a load it was never built to lift: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV).
And the reviving word of Galatians 6 is that some weights were never meant to be carried by one man, and that lifting them for each other is how the law of Christ gets kept.

sections.heading: What Grace Looks Like on a Tuesday
pulls: You probably fail in both directions at once — shouldering crushing weights in silence while trying to hand off packs you were built to carry.
paras: Paul has told the Galatians to keep in step with the Spirit. Now he shows them what that looks like in a real congregation, on an ordinary week, when a brother has fallen.
Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.

Notice the assumption built into the first clause: a man will be caught. Paul does not write if a congregation should ever face this unfortunate situation. He writes as a pastor who knows that in any real church, on any given month, someone is in the ditch.

And notice who is assigned the work. You who are spiritual — which in the immediate context means those walking in the fruit of chapter five, the men with gentleness and self-control. Restoration is not given to the most doctrinally precise. It is given to the gentlest.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: SETTING A BONE
paras: The word behind restore was used for setting a broken bone and for mending a net. Both images assume the same two things: that the thing is worth repairing, and that the repair requires skill.

That reframes the whole task. A man who has fallen is not garbage to be discarded and not a problem to be contained. He is a fracture to be set — and anyone who has seen a bone set knows it is done firmly, precisely, and with great care for the pain involved.

And Paul attaches a safeguard that is easy to skip: looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. The verb is singular in a sentence otherwise addressed to a group — each man, watch yourself. The one who confronts sin without a sober awareness of his own capacity for it will do more damage than the sin did.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: TWO WORDS FOR WEIGHT
paras: Then Paul sets two statements side by side that look like a contradiction until you check the Greek. Bear one another’s burdens. And three verses later: each man will bear his own burden.
They are different words. The first is baros — a crushing weight, more than one man can lift. The second is phortion — the ordinary pack a man carries on the road, sized to him.

So there is no contradiction. There are burdens no man was meant to carry alone, and there are responsibilities no man may hand to someone else. Christian community is largely a matter of knowing which is which — and you probably fail in both directions at once, shouldering crushing weights in silence while trying to hand off packs you were built to carry.

And notice what Paul calls the lifting: so fulfill the law of Christ. Having spent five chapters removing the law as a means of acceptance, he hands you a law again — but it is the law of a Person, and it is kept by carrying weight for people.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: GOD IS NOT MOCKED
paras: Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.

The verb behind mocked means to turn up one’s nose — to sneer. Men imagine they can live one way and harvest another, that the ordinary laws of the moral universe will be quietly suspended in their case. Paul says the assumption is a sneer at God, and God does not accept it.
What a man sows, he reaps. Not to earn salvation — the letter has settled that permanently. But because God has built the world this way, and grace does not repeal the harvest.

And the two soils are named plainly: he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life. Seed goes into the ground unseen. That is precisely what makes it dangerous, and precisely what makes small faithfulness worth more than it looks.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE WEARINESS PAUL EXPECTS
paras: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.

Notice that Paul assumes the weariness. He does not treat it as a mark of weak faith or a sign that something has gone wrong. He treats it as an ordinary hazard of a long obedience, and he speaks to it directly.
Doing good is tiring. The harvest is usually invisible. And the temptation to quit rarely comes from unbelief — it comes from exhaustion, which is a different problem and needs a different answer.

Paul’s answer is a season. We will reap in due season — God’s season, not yours. A farmer who dug up his seed every week to check on it would never eat. Much of the good you do you will not see the fruit of until the last day, and the faith that keeps sowing without seeing is precisely the faith this letter has commended from chapter one.

stations.verse: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
stations.question: When someone falls, is my instinct to contain the damage — or to set the bone?
stations.gloss: to mend; to set a fracture; to put back into working order
body: Katartizō means to restore something to its proper condition. Matthew uses it of James and John mending their nets. In medical writing it was the standard term for setting a dislocated joint or a broken bone.

Both pictures carry the same assumptions. The object is valuable, the damage is real, and the repair takes skill rather than sentiment. Nobody sets a bone by wishing it well, and nobody sets one by force either.

Which is why Paul specifies the manner: in a spirit of gentleness. Anyone who has watched a fracture set knows the work is firm, but the firmness serves the healing. The dust says a fallen brother is a liability. Katartizō says he is a fracture, and fractures are set by men who know how easily they themselves break.
stations.live: Name the person in your life who has fallen and whom you have been quietly avoiding. Go to him this week as a man setting a bone, not filing a report.

stations.verse: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
stations.question: What am I carrying alone that was never sized for one man?
stations.gloss: a crushing weight; a load heavier than one man can carry
body: Baros denotes heaviness — real, oppressive weight. Matthew uses it of laborers who bore the burden and heat of the day. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians of an eternal weight of glory, where the same word turns from oppression to substance.
It is not the word for ordinary responsibility. It is the word for a load that flattens. And Paul’s command is to get underneath other men’s: bear one another’s burdens.

Then he calls that lifting the fulfilling of the law of Christ. Having removed the law as a ladder, Paul gives it back as a description — and the description is a Person who bore a weight no man could lift. Getting under a brother’s load is how a man shows whose he is.
stations.live: Tell one trustworthy man the thing you have been carrying alone. Not the summary — the actual weight.

stations.verse: For each man will bear his own burden.
stations.question: What responsibility have I been trying to hand to someone else that is properly mine?
stations.gloss: a pack; the load a man is expected to carry himself
body: Phortion is a diminutive from phortos, a ship’s cargo. It denotes a load proportioned to the bearer — a man’s pack on the road, or the cargo assigned to a ship. Jesus uses it when He says my burden is light.

So the apparent contradiction with verse two dissolves once the words are distinguished. Baros is a weight that flattens a man; phortion is the pack he was issued. Carry each other’s baros. Do not try to give away your phortion. Both errors are common and both are damaging. A man who hands off his own pack becomes a burden to everyone near him. A man who refuses help with a crushing weight robs his brothers of the very work Christ assigned them.
stations.live: Identify one responsibility you have been quietly outsourcing — to a spouse, a friend, a pastor. Take it back this week and carry your own pack.

stations.verse: Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.
stations.question: Where am I living as though the ordinary harvest will be suspended in my case?
stations.gloss: to turn up the nose at; to sneer
stations.xref: GALATIANS 6:7 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT
body: Myktērizō comes from myktēr, the nostril. It means literally to turn up the nose — to sneer. It appears only here in the New Testament.

Paul is describing an attitude rather than an argument. Nobody announces that he expects the moral order to be suspended for him. He simply lives as though it will — sowing in one field and confidently expecting a harvest from another. And Paul’s answer is not a threat but a fact about the world: God is not mocked. You cannot sneer at a harvest law any more than at gravity. Grace forgives the sower fully and does not repeal the field.
stations.live: Name one field you have been sowing in while hoping for a harvest from somewhere else. Stop scattering that seed this week.

stations.verse: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.
stations.question: Where has my quitting been about exhaustion rather than unbelief?
stations.gloss: to lose heart; to grow weary and give in to discouragement
body: Enkakeō joins en with kakos, bad — to give in to what is bad in a situation, hence to lose heart. It is not primarily about doubting God’s truth. It is about running out of stamina.

Paul uses it of himself and his companions twice in one chapter of 2 Corinthians: “we don’t faint.” Luke uses it when Jesus tells a parable “that they must always pray, and not give up.” The New Testament assumes this is a normal hazard, not an exotic failure.

Which is why the remedy Paul offers is not a rebuke but a season. “We will reap in due season” — God’s timing, not yours. The weary man does not need to be told he is faithless. He needs to be told the harvest is real and the clock is not his.
stations.live: Name the good work you are closest to abandoning. Do not evaluate it this week — just do it once more, and leave the season to God.

practices.title: TELL ONE MAN THE WEIGHT
practices.body: Name the thing you have been carrying alone and tell one trustworthy man the actual weight of it, not the summary. Paul calls it a baros — a load that flattens. It was never sized for one set of shoulders.

practices.title: TAKE BACK YOUR PACK
practices.body: Now the other direction. Identify one responsibility you have been quietly outsourcing to a spouse, a friend, a pastor. Carry your own phortion this week without complaint or announcement.

practices.title: SET ONE BONE
practices.body: Go to the person who has fallen and whom you have been avoiding. Go gently, watching yourself, and go to restore rather than to assess. A fracture is set firmly by someone who knows how easily he breaks.

practices.title: NAME THE FIELD
practices.body: Find the place where you are sowing in one soil and hoping for a harvest from another. Say it plainly and stop scattering that seed. God forgives the sower completely and does not suspend the field.

practices.title: DO IT ONCE MORE
practices.body: Name the good work you are closest to quitting. Do not evaluate its results this week. Just do it one more time, and let the season belong to God — a farmer who digs up his seed to check on it never eats.

title: Bear One Another’s Burdens
subtitle: from dust to the law of Christ
keyVerse: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

passage.text: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.
For each man will bear his own burden.
But let him who is taught in the word share all good things with him who teaches.
Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.
For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about learning which weights are yours and which are not — and about staying in the field long enough to see a season you do not control.
lifePulls: Grace forgives the sower fully and does not repeal the field.
prayer: Lord Jesus, You bore a weight I could never lift. Show me which load is mine to carry and which I was never meant to carry alone. Give me a gentle hand for the brother who has fallen, and keep me watching myself while I help him. Put me under someone else’s burden today. When I grow weary of doing good, remind me that the harvest keeps Your calendar, not mine. Amen.
prayerLines: Lord Jesus, You bore a weight I could never lift.
Show me which load is mine to carry
and which I was never meant to carry alone.
Give me a gentle hand for the brother who has fallen,
and keep me watching myself while I help him.
Put me under someone else’s burden today.
When I grow weary of doing good,
remind me that the harvest keeps Your calendar, not mine. Amen.
bottomLine: Paul assumes a man will be caught, so he gives the work of restoring him to the gentle, each man watching himself. Bear one another’s crushing loads, carry your own pack, and so fulfill the law of Christ, who got under a weight no man could lift. The harvest is real and keeps God’s calendar, so do not give up before the season He has set.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the load you have been carrying in silence and onto the men God put around you to help lift it. You have called it strength. You have called it not wanting to be a burden. But Paul has a word for what you are under, and it is not the word for a pack a man carries — it is the word for a weight that flattens him, and it was never sized for one set of shoulders.

And look at what he calls the lifting. So fulfill the law of Christ. After five chapters spent tearing the law down as a ladder, he hands it back as a portrait — and the portrait is a Man who got underneath a weight that would have crushed any man and carried it up a hill. You do not keep His law by achieving. You keep it by stooping.

So go and set a bone this week. There is someone you have been avoiding because he fell, and the avoiding feels like discretion. It is not. He is a fracture, not a liability, and fractures are set by men who know exactly how easily they break themselves — which is why the work is given to the gentle and never to the impressed.

And do not grow weary. The seed goes in where you cannot see it. The seed keeps a calendar you did not write. The seed does not need you digging it up every week to check on it. Paul says it plainly: “we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.” Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to, and stay in the field.
closingVerse: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
carry: What have you been carrying alone and calling it strength — when Christ has put men around you whose obedience this week is to get underneath it with you?

paras: Every man has a sentence he reaches for when he needs to feel like himself again. It is usually short, and it is usually about something he has done, built, survived, or is known for. He does not say it out loud. He just runs it quietly when the ground gets unstable.

That sentence is doing more work than he realizes. It is where he goes to establish that he is worth something — and because it rests on a thing that can be lost, he has to keep the thing alive. Which is exhausting, and which explains a great deal about how he spends his weeks.

Here is where the dust lies to you. It never tells you that you have no worth. It offers you a place to find some — a record, a role, a reputation — and then requires you to defend it forever. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul worn out by that maintenance: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV).
And the reviving word of Galatians 6 is that there is exactly one thing left in the universe worth boasting in, and it is a Roman execution.

sections.heading: A Man Takes the Pen
pulls: A man who has actually seen the cross stops needing the world’s applause and stops fearing its rejection — and those two freedoms always arrive together.
paras: See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand.

Paul did not always hold the pen; Romans names the man who wrote that letter down for him. Here, at the close, he takes it himself, and he tells you he is writing in large letters — a man leaning over the table, pressing hard, making the last words unmistakable.

It is the ancient equivalent of raising your voice at the end. Whatever else these Galatians forget, they are not going to miss this. And what he writes in that heavy hand is a final exposure of his opponents, followed by the sentence that summarizes his entire life.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE MOTIVE UNDERNEATH THE THEOLOGY
paras: As many as desire to make a good impression in the flesh compel you to be circumcised; just so they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.
Paul finally names what has been driving the whole crisis, and it is not doctrinal conviction. It is two things: the desire to make a good showing, and the desire to avoid trouble.

The Judaizers wanted a mark they could count and display. They wanted a report they could take back to Jerusalem. And they wanted to sidestep the hostility that comes with preaching a bare cross — because a message that lets men contribute has always been more welcome than one that tells them they bring nothing.

Then Paul exposes the inconsistency: for even they who receive circumcision don’t keep the law themselves, but they desire to have you circumcised, that they may boast in your flesh. Their zeal for the law was never about the law. They were collecting credentials, and the credentials were other men.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE ONLY THING LEFT TO BOAST IN
paras: But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.

This may be the summary of Paul’s entire life. Everything the world offers as a reason for boasting is dead to him, and he is dead to it. The cross has come between them, and a crucifixion is not a temporary estrangement.

Consider what he is giving up. Paul had credentials that would have impressed anyone in his world — tribe, training, blamelessness under the law, a rabbinical pedigree. He lists them in Philippians and then calls them refuse.

And notice the double death. The world has been crucified to me — its verdict on him no longer carries weight. And I to the world — his standing in its eyes is gone, and he has stopped applying for it. A man who has actually seen the cross stops needing the world’s applause and stops fearing its rejection, and those two freedoms always arrive together.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: WHAT ACTUALLY COUNTS NOW
paras: For in Christ Jesus neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.

Paul said something almost identical back in chapter five, where the answer was faith working through love. Here the answer is a new creation. They are not two answers; they are the inside and the outside of one thing.

Every category that once told a man who he was and what he was worth has been relativized. Circumcised or not, Jew or Greek, accomplished or ruined — none of it counts, because God has done something that was not there before.

And a new creation is not a renovated one. Paul is reaching for the language of Genesis: God speaking into a void and calling into existence what did not exist. That is what happened in you. Not an improvement of the old man, but a making.

Then the benediction: as many as walk by this rule, peace and mercy be on them, and on God’s Israel. The rule is the new creation, and the people who walk by it are the Israel of God — Jew and Gentile together, defined by the cross rather than by the flesh.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: TWO KINDS OF MARKS
paras: From now on, let no one cause me any trouble, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body.

The contrast with verse twelve is deliberate and devastating. The Judaizers wanted a mark in the flesh they could display — evidence of their success, and protection from persecution. Paul says he has marks too.

Paul does not say which scars he means. He does not need to. By his own count to the Corinthians he had been beaten with rods three times and stoned once. He is not boasting in his suffering; he is pointing out the difference between a mark that advertises a man and a mark that proves whose he is.

And then the last line, and it is the first line again: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen. Grace on the first page, grace on the last, and everything in between is the defense of what stands between those two bookends.

stations.verse: As many as desire to make a good impression in the flesh compel you to be circumcised; just so they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.
stations.question: How much of my spiritual activity is actually about how it looks?
stations.gloss: to present a good face; to make a fair outward showing
stations.xref: GALATIANS 6:12 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT
body: Euprosōpeō joins eu, well, to prosōpon, face. It means to look good in the face — to present well. It occurs only here in the New Testament, and Paul adds the decisive qualifier: in the flesh.

Prosōpon was also the word for a mask worn by an actor. That association hangs over the verse. These men were not preaching a conviction; they were managing an appearance, and the appearance required other men’s bodies to sustain it.

Which is why Paul pairs it with the second motive: so they may not be persecuted for the cross. Wanting to look good and wanting to avoid cost are almost always the same impulse, and together they have corrupted more theology than open unbelief ever has.
stations.live: Name one thing you do spiritually that you would stop doing if no one ever knew about it. Do it in secret this week, or do not do it at all.

stations.verse: But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
stations.question: What is the sentence I run quietly when I need to feel like I am worth something?
stations.gloss: to boast; to rest one’s confidence and identity in something
body: Kauchaomai is more than bragging. In Paul it means to locate your confidence somewhere — to have a ground on which you stand and from which you assess your own worth. Every man boasts in something, whether or not he ever says it aloud.

So the question is never whether you will boast but where. Jeremiah drew the line and Paul quotes it twice: he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord. The alternatives are not humility and pride. They are two different foundations.

And Paul chooses the least impressive object available: a Roman execution. He had credentials that would have played well in any room of his world, and he called them refuse, because a boast that rests on something you can lose has to be defended forever.
stations.live: Write the sentence you run when you need to feel worth something. Then write the cross beside it, and ask which one requires you to keep something alive.

stations.verse: For in Christ Jesus neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.
stations.question: Am I asking God to improve the old man — when He has already made a new one?
stations.gloss: creation; the act of founding or bringing into existence
body: Ktisis comes from ktizō, to found or create. In Greek it was used of founding a city — establishing something that did not exist before. In the New Testament it belongs to God’s creative work, never to human manufacture.

That is the weight Paul puts on the phrase. Not a reformed man, not a man with better habits, but a new creation — the vocabulary of Genesis, of a God who speaks into a void and calls into being what was not there.

And it is the final answer to a letter about credentials. Circumcision counts for nothing and uncircumcision counts for nothing, because both are facts about the old order. What counts is that God has made something. You are not a renovation. You are a founding.
stations.live: Stop asking God this week to improve the man you have been. Ask Him instead to let you live as the man He has already made.

stations.verse: As many as walk by this rule, peace and mercy be on them, and on God’s Israel.
stations.question: What am I actually measuring my life against — and would I say it out loud?
stations.gloss: a measuring rod; a standard against which a thing is judged straight
body: Kanōn is a rod or measuring rule — the word is related to kanna, a reed — and from there it came to mean any fixed standard. It is the word behind the English canon — the rule by which the church measures Scripture itself.
Paul pairs it here with the verb for walking in rank, the same one from chapter five. Men who keep step by this measuring rod — by the new creation, not by the flesh — receive peace and mercy.

And he lays that blessing on God’s Israel: Jew and Gentile together, defined by the cross rather than by descent. It is the last blow against a letter’s worth of credentialism. The measuring rod is not your pedigree. It is what God has made.
stations.live: Name the rod you have actually been measuring yourself against this year. If it is not the new creation, retire it this week.

stations.verse: From now on, let no one cause me any trouble, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body.
stations.question: What has following Christ actually cost me — and am I ashamed of it or settled in it?
stations.gloss: a brand; a mark burned into the body to show ownership
stations.xref: GALATIANS 6:17 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT
body: Stigma appears only here in the New Testament. It means a mark pricked or branded into the skin — a brand that stays.

Paul does not say which scars he means, but he had listed enough of them for the Corinthians: beaten with rods three times, stoned once. He calls them the marks of the Lord Jesus. He is not romanticizing suffering. He is showing whose he is.

And the contrast with verse twelve is exact. His opponents wanted a mark in the flesh that would advertise their success and spare them persecution. Paul carries a mark that advertises nothing and cost him everything, and it proves the one thing theirs never could: whose he is.
stations.live: Name one cost you have paid for following Christ and stop apologizing for it. It is not a wound to explain away. It is a mark of ownership.

practices.title: WRITE YOUR BOAST
practices.body: Write the sentence you run quietly when you need to feel worth something. Then write the cross beside it. Ask which one requires you to keep something alive, and which one was finished without you.

practices.title: DO ONE THING IN SECRET
practices.body: Name a spiritual activity you would abandon if no one ever knew. Do it this week with no possibility of it being seen — or do not do it at all. Euprosōpeō is a mask word, and masks come off best in private.

practices.title: RETIRE THE MEASURING ROD
practices.body: Name what you have actually been measuring your life against this year: income, comparison, output, someone’s approval. If it is not the new creation, set it down and say what the real rule is.

practices.title: OWN THE SCAR
practices.body: Name one cost you have paid for following Christ that you usually explain away or minimize in conversation. Stop apologizing for it this week. It is not a wound. It is a brand.

practices.title: CLOSE WITH GRACE
practices.body: The letter opens and closes with the same word. Take one relationship where you have been keeping a ledger and close the account this week the way Paul closes his letter — grace, and nothing owed.

title: Boasting Only in the Cross
subtitle: from dust to a new creation

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about finding the sentence you have been boasting in, and letting the cross come between you and a world whose verdict you have been quietly applying for.
lifePulls: You are not a renovation. You are a founding.
prayer: Lord Jesus, I will boast in nothing but Your cross. Take the sentence I keep running to feel like somebody, and let it die with the world I was crucified to. I am not the old man improved; I am a new creation. Let me walk by that rule today, and let the marks I carry show whose I am. Amen.

bottomLine: Paul takes the pen and names what drove the whole crisis: men who wanted a good showing in the flesh and wanted to escape persecution for the cross. Against them he sets one boast — the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to him and he to the world. What counts now is not circumcision or uncircumcision but a new creation, and the marks he carries show whose he is.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the sentence you have been running to feel like somebody and onto the only ground that will still be holding on the last day. You know the sentence. It is short, it is about something you did or built or survived, and you have to keep it alive — which is why you are tired in a way that sleep does not touch.

Paul had better material than yours and counted it “nothing but refuse.” He had the tribe. He had the training. He had a blamelessness under the law that would have opened any door in his world. He set the whole of it down and picked up the least impressive object available: a Roman cross. Far be it from me to boast, he says, except in the cross.

And see what the cross did for him, because it will do the same for you. The world crucified to me, and I to the world — two deaths, one on each side. Its applause cannot reach him and its contempt cannot wound him, and those two freedoms have never once arrived separately. A man who stops needing the verdict stops fearing it.

So walk by the new rule. Not circumcision, not uncircumcision, not any credential the old order still trades in — a new creation, spoken into being by the God who calls into existence the things that do not exist. You are not the old man improved. You are something made. And the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, which opened this letter and now closes it, be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
closingVerse: But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
carry: What sentence have you been running to prove you are worth something, when the cross is the only ground you need?
